opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this was a really humbling experience, honestly. When we were building photonic chips for quantum computing, we had these programmable meshes of interferometers that could route light from any input to any output, and they were fast. We could reconfigure them in nanoseconds. So the naive thought was: this is obviously a great network switch. Data centers move enormous amounts of data, and here's something that switches light directly without converting it back to electronics.

What I learned pretty quickly, once I started talking to people who actually run these networks, is that raw switching speed wasn't the bottleneck I thought it was. The things that mattered were much less glamorous: reliability, cost per port, power, how many ports you could scale to, and above all how the thing fits into the existing ecosystem. A data center network is a huge operational system. If your switch needs exotic calibration, or behaves differently when the temperature drifts, or makes the software stack harder to manage, that's a non-starter no matter how elegant the physics is.

The other big shift was realizing that the traffic patterns matter more than the hardware. In quantum computing you care about precise, coherent control of a fairly small number of modes. In a data center you have thousands of machines with bursty, messy, unpredictable traffic, and the real question is whether you can schedule and reconfigure fast enough to match what the workload is doing. That's a systems and software problem as much as an optics problem.

So I came in thinking, "I have a better hammer," and left understanding that you have to start from what the network actually needs and work backward. That perspective, starting from the workload instead of the technology, has stuck with me ever since, especially now that we're thinking about networks for large-scale AI training, where communication patterns are much more structured and that structure is something you can actually exploit.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is one of those cases where you walk in with a hypothesis that turns out to be almost exactly backwards, and the interesting part is how you figure that out.

The chips we were building for quantum computing were these programmable photonic circuits. You've got a mesh of interferometers, you can route light anywhere you want, and the whole design philosophy is about precision. Low loss, very controlled phase, every component behaving as close to ideally as you can get it. And so the naive pitch is, well, a data center switch is just routing light from input port to output port, we already do that, let's go sell it.

The first thing that changed was my sense of what "switching" even means in that world. I was thinking of a switch like a circuit. You set up a path, light goes down it. But a data center is packet-based. The traffic is bursty, it's short-lived, it's changing on the order of microseconds or less. And our devices reconfigured on timescales that were fine for a lab experiment and completely wrong for that. So the question stopped being "can we route light" and became "can we reconfigure fast enough that the network doesn't notice," and that is a totally different engineering problem.

The second thing, and this is the one that really stuck with me, is that nobody in a data center cares about the switch in isolation. They care about the whole stack. Transceivers, the electrical interface, how you do the control plane, what happens when something fails, what the power draw is per bit. I'd spent years optimizing a device metric, and then I'd go talk to someone running a cluster and they'd ask, okay, what does it cost me in watts and dollars per port, and what happens at three in the morning when a laser dies. And I didn't have good answers, because that's not what the quantum work had trained me to think about.

And then the third piece was realizing that the actual pressure in those networks isn't where I expected. I assumed it was bandwidth. It's partly that, but the thing people were really wrestling with was how traffic patterns were changing, especially as the workloads moved toward large distributed training. You get these very structured, very predictable flows between groups of machines, and that's actually where optical circuit switching starts to make sense again. Not as a general-purpose packet switch, but as a way to reconfigure the physical topology to match the job. So the lesson was less "our chip is a switch" and more "there's a specific layer in the network where a slow, lossless, reconfigurable optical fabric is exactly the right tool, and you have to design for that layer rather than trying to replace everything."

So I'd say the biggest shift was going from thinking about the device to thinking about the system, and then being honest about where the device actually fits.

astra-6.text:
The big shift was from thinking about the switching device to thinking about the whole network. When you’re working on an optical chip, it’s natural to focus on things like how fast it switches and how much light you lose going through it. But a data center doesn’t need a fast switch in isolation. It needs applications to move data reliably and efficiently.

So the question becomes: What traffic are you trying to carry? How long do those connections need to last? How do you coordinate changing an optical connection with the computers sending data? A device can look great on its own and still be difficult to use in a real system.

That changed how I thought about the opportunity. It wasn’t simply, ‘Can we use this chip as a network switch?’ It was, ‘Can we build a network around this capability that actually makes the workload run better?’

sol-6.1.text:
The big shift was realizing that a data center doesn’t just need a switch that’s fast. It needs a network that delivers useful bandwidth reliably, at the right cost and power, for the traffic the computers actually generate.

Coming from quantum computing, we were thinking about how to control light on a chip. And that suggested a natural question: could we use that control to connect computers optically? But then you have to understand when those connections need to change, how long they can stay in place, and what happens to the data while you’re reconfiguring them.

So the problem became much more about the whole system. A really impressive optical device is only useful if the network architecture and the software can take advantage of it. That changed how we thought about what we needed to build.
